# Implement block: Prism Spectrum Player (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Prism Spectrum Player" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A night-time "now playing" screen for "Low Tide Lanterns" by Iva North, from the album Glasshouse. A white beam rises from the lower left into a glass prism and leaves as a rainbow fan of twelve spectral bands, and each band is an equaliser bar whose length follows the music, with dust motes glinting in the light. Drag across the prism to turn it: the fan swings and opens wider behind it. The play button brightens the beam and lifts the bars, or dims them back down; a scrubber, back and forward 5 s, skip buttons and an up-next card complete the player.

**Motion.** The hero is one full-screen runtime shader: an indigo glasshouse backdrop (3-stop gradient, faint arched window frame, vignette, 3.5 % grain), the incoming beam (2.2 pt core, 11 pt halo) aimed at the middle of the prism's left face, the prism as an equilateral-triangle SDF (side 204 pt at 393 pt wide) with refracted backdrop, the beam inside it splitting towards the exit, inner-edge glow, a bevel 6 pt in, a sheen band that slides with the turn, a 1 pt outline highlight and star glints on the three corners, and the fan from the middle of the right face. The fan is cut into 12 bands (red least deviated, violet most; 70 % bar, 30 % gap, white near the apex). Each band's length runs from 48 pt to the longest that fits (≤ 214 pt), set by a level computed in the shader from the clock: 0.40 + three sines at whole multiples of the 8 s loop (2–4, 7–12, 19–27 per loop, seeded per band) + a 120 BPM kick stronger in the low bands; paused, the levels fall to a gentle arch. Bars have a bright 2.4 pt cap and a faint tail; light is added and soft-clipped (1 − e^−x). Fan direction = 0.4 rad + 1.7 × the fan's angle; spread = 0.48 rad × (1 + 0.9·|angle| / 25°) × (0.78 + 0.22 × playing). Colours are converted from sRGB to Display P3 on iOS. Controls are drawn in the same Canvas (static ones in a Picture recorded once, scrubber/times/play button per frame); the play icon morphs between play and pause by moving the vertices of two quads.
autoPlay (LOOP 8 s): 0–1.2 rest (paused, beam at 40 %, short dim bars); 1.08–1.32 play pressed (scale 0.92); 1.2–1.8 beam up, bars rise, fan opens (ease-out cubic), icon morphs 1.2–1.45; 1.8–6.4 playing, elapsed 1:12 → 1:17; 3.0–5.6 the prism turns 0 → +18° → 0 → −18° → 0 (sine of an ease-in-out sweep) with the fan 90 ms behind; 6.28–6.52 pause pressed, 6.4–7.0 beam dims and bars fall (ease-in-out cubic); 6.95–7.25 back-5 pressed and 7.0–7.7 the scrubber glides back to 1:12; 7.0–8.0 rest.
Touch: horizontal drag turns the prism 0.0042 rad per pt, limited to ±25° with a rubber band past it (selection haptic at the limit); on release it springs (450 ms, damping ratio 0.8) to where its momentum points (velocity × 0.12 s, clamped). The fan follows the prism on a spring (stiffness 420, damping ratio 0.72). Play/pause fades beam and bars over 600 ms (ease-in-out) with a light haptic; the button dips to 0.92 on press-in (110 ms) and springs back. 2 s after the last touch everything eases to rest in 0.8 s and the loop restarts; the bars, motes and glints keep their own clock so nothing jumps.
Reduced motion: no loop; the prism still turns under the finger without the lagging fan, play/pause fades in 300 ms.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [PrismSpectrumPlayerDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PrismSpectrumPlayer/PrismSpectrumPlayerDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [PrismSpectrumPlayer.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PrismSpectrumPlayer/PrismSpectrumPlayer.metal)
- [PrismSpectrumPlayer.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PrismSpectrumPlayer/PrismSpectrumPlayer.swift)
- [PrismSpectrumPlayerArt.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PrismSpectrumPlayer/PrismSpectrumPlayerArt.swift)
- [PrismSpectrumPlayerMotion.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Media/PrismSpectrumPlayer/PrismSpectrumPlayerMotion.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
